emergency.general: Call 911 for all emergencies (nationwide). Alternatively, use 107 for ambulance, 101 for police, or 100 for fire. Operators primarily speak Spanish — if you don't speak Spanish, try to have a local or hotel staff assist, or use a translation app. In Buenos Aires, tourist police can help in English.

healthcare.summary: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to Argentina. Emergency numbers (107/101/911), pharmacy tips, restricted medications, vaccination requirements, and travel insurance advice.

medications.prescriptionRules: A prescription is required for most prescription medications. Antibiotics and many drugs are available OTC with less strict enforcement than in the US. Carry all medications in original packaging with a doctor's note in Spanish or English.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD stimulant medications (Adderall, Ritalin, Vyvanse)
restrictedMeds.note: Stimulants are controlled substances in Argentina. Bring original prescription, doctor's letter, and only the amount needed. Declare to customs. A local prescription may be needed for larger quantities.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine is controlled. Some codeine products require prescription. Carry alternatives if possible.

restrictedMeds.name: Psychotropic medications (diazepam, alprazolam, etc.)
restrictedMeds.note: Benzodiazepines require documentation. Bring a doctor's letter explaining medical necessity.

restrictedMeds.name: Methylphenidate (Ritalin/Concerta)
restrictedMeds.note: Bring documentation and only the amount needed for your stay.

medications.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in Spanish or English listing all medications with generic names. Keep medications in original packaging. For controlled substances, carry original prescriptions and a note explaining medical necessity. Spanish translations are helpful.
medications.generalAdvice: Argentina follows international drug conventions but enforcement at customs is relatively relaxed for personal-use medications. Carry all medications in original packaging with a doctor's letter — Spanish translation is helpful. Controlled substances (stimulants, benzodiazepines, codeine) should be declared at customs with supporting prescriptions and only in quantities needed for your stay.

connectivity.simOptions: Claro, Movistar, or Personal prepaid SIMs at airport or city shops. Bring passport. Data is reasonably priced. Cash payments often cheaper than card.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi at most cafes, restaurants, and hotels in Buenos Aires. Quality good in major cities, limited in rural Patagonia.
connectivity.bestOption: Claro prepaid SIM for best coverage. Buy at Buenos Aires airport. eSIM via Airalo as backup. Note: bring US dollars — better exchange rate on 'blue dollar' market.

cultural.tipping: 10% at restaurants is customary. Round up for taxis. Tip hotel porters AR$500-1000. Propina (tip) jars common at cafes.
cultural.dressCode: Smart casual in Buenos Aires — Argentines are stylish. Casual elsewhere. No special religious dress codes.
cultural.greetings: One kiss on the right cheek for everyone (men-men, men-women, women-women). Even at first meeting. Handshake only in very formal business.
taboos: Comparing Argentina to other Latin American countries negatively
Rushing meals — dinner starts at 9-10 PM and is a social event
Being punctual to social events (arrive 30-60 min late)
cultural.haggling: Not common at shops or restaurants. Acceptable at artisan markets and when paying cash (ask for 'descuento en efectivo').

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 90 days visa-free. UK, EU, Australia, Canada also visa-free. Reciprocity fee eliminated.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: October-April (spring/summer). Patagonia: December-February. Buenos Aires: March-May, September-November (mild). Ski season: June-September.

steps: File a police report immediately — get the report number, you will need it
Contact the US Embassy or nearest consulate: Contact the nearest US Embassy
Bring the police report + any ID you have (driver's license, copy of passport)
Apply for an Emergency Passport (usually issued within 1-2 business days)
Notify your travel insurance and airline of the situation
stolenPassport.notes: Keep a digital copy of your passport in cloud storage (Google Photos, iCloud) and email yourself a scan before travel.

steps: Go to the nearest police station (or call 101)
Bring ID or a copy of your passport if available
Request a written report — ask for an English copy or certified translation if needed
Keep the report number safe — required for insurance claims
For theft: list all stolen items with approximate values
policeReport.notes: In many countries, tourist police stations are available in major cities — they have English-speaking staff. Ask your hotel concierge for the nearest tourist police.

steps: If involved in an accident: do not move vehicles if anyone is injured
Call police (101) and ambulance (107) if there are injuries
Exchange contact, license, and insurance details with other parties
Document the scene with photos before moving vehicles
Contact your rental car company's emergency line
Contact your travel insurance's 24h assistance line
roadsideAssistance.notes: Traffic drives on the RIGHT. An International Driving Permit (IDP) is recommended for most foreign licenses. Rental vehicles are available at major airports and cities.
